claims.text: The initial material is a quaternary equiatomic alloy with an FCC crystal structure.
Plastic deformation under uniaxial tension is governed by dislocation glide on {111} planes.
Yield strength becomes insensitive to strain rate below a critical strain-rate threshold.
At low strain rates, thermal activation is insufficient to overcome lattice friction.
Rate independence requires the absence of a stress-induced phase transformation.
Maintaining room temperature or another fixed sub-transformation temperature isolates the mechanical response.
Dislocation density and mobility within the FCC lattice mediate the tensile response.
The operative mechanism is thermally activated dislocation glide overcoming the Peierls barrier and solute drag.
Yield strength increases with strain rate in the high-rate regime.
The low-rate yield-strength plateau results from negligible thermal activation or a shift to athermal glide.
Stress-induced FCC-to-HCP/BCC transformation or twinning would alter the deformation mechanism.
Emergence of non-FCC diffraction peaks below the predicted yield point would indicate transformation before dislocation-based yielding.
X-ray line broadening can be used to determine dislocation density.
Thermal activation is impossible at very high strain rates.
Rate-independent yield strength at very high strain rates would suggest a purely athermal mechanism other than standard dislocation glide, such as immediate phase transformation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes the low-rate plateau to thermal activation being insufficient to overcome lattice friction, while the stated operative mechanism requires thermally activated glide to overcome that friction.

Thermal activation is described as negligible or insufficient at low strain rates and also as impossible at very high strain rates, leaving no coherent rate regime for the asserted thermally activated mechanism.
